question: How do input layout, attention depth, width, and numerical precision control whether a shallow transformer can evaluate an arbitrary finite key-value function at a queried key?

key_findings.claim: A one-head, one-layer hard-attention transformer with constant embedding dimension and logarithmic precision can evaluate the function whenever key identity is colocated with its value or recoverable from position.
key_findings.evidence: Theorems 3.1-3.3 give explicit circular encodings of integers and dot-product selectors. They cover same-position ordered or permuted key-value pairs, values placed in key order with no explicit keys, and consecutive ordered keys and values whose positions redundantly determine the key. Each construction has dimension four, one head, and O(log n) precision.

key_findings.claim: When permuted keys and values occupy separate consecutive positions, exact one-layer softmax evaluation has a tight communication-size requirement of order n log n under the stated finite-precision model.
key_findings.evidence: The communication reduction separates the value sequence, known to Alice, from the key permutation, known to Bob. Exact evaluation can transmit an arbitrary n-symbol value sequence, requiring n log_2 n bits; simulation of a one-layer transformer transmits at most 3hdp bits. Theorem 3.6 gives hdp at least n log n/3, and Theorem 3.7 constructs a softmax model with dimension 2n+2 and O(log n) precision.

key_findings.claim: A second attention layer restores a concise construction for the difficult separated-and-permuted layout by first binding each key to its adjacent value and then performing ordinary lookup.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 3.12 uses one head, dimension seven, logarithmic precision, and a residual in layer one. The first hard-attention layer copies each even-position key into the following odd value position; the second layer selects the newly colocated pair matching the target key and returns its value.

key_findings.claim: The empirical results qualitatively separate easy and difficult layouts, but they do not test the theorem's arbitrary-function distribution.
key_findings.evidence: Every trained example uses a random permutation of [n] as the function, so every output value occurs exactly once. The theory ranges over all n^n functions, including repeated and missing values. Permutation-only training makes the empirical task smaller and structurally more regular, especially for n=2 and n=5 where the paper says all possible inputs are repeatedly observed.

anchors.section: 4.1-4.2, empirical data generation and sequence counts

key_findings.claim: The claimed theory-learnability alignment is suggestive rather than a validation of the constructions or lower bound.
key_findings.evidence: The positive proofs use hand-designed circular embeddings and leftmost hard attention, whereas experiments learn token and position embeddings in softmax transformers with residuals. Conversely, every tested difficult-layout model is compatible with the asymptotic hdp lower bound, as the authors acknowledge. Thus success or failure under Adam is not predicted quantitatively by the proved bound.

key_findings.claim: Depth helps optimization on the difficult layout at moderate width, but neither depth nor greater dimension guarantees learning.
key_findings.evidence: For n=20 and token dimensions 16 or 32, two-layer models reach about 99.9-100% best-run accuracy while one-layer models peak at 26.5% and 69.8%. Yet at dimensions 100 and 200, both depths remain near chance or low accuracy. Across easier layouts, many settings are bimodal: for example, same-position permuted keys at dimension eight have 100% maximum but only 24.83% mean accuracy over five seeds.

key_findings.claim: Theorem 3.8's 'hard attention of any c-size' wording is only justified for the paper's specialized single-head model, not unrestricted multi-head hard attention.
key_findings.evidence: Section 2.2 explicitly specializes the hard-attention definition to one head, and Appendix E reasons about one selected or averaged attention output. With O(n) fixed-position hard-attention heads, however, a target position can copy every input token and a sufficiently large MLP can perform the lookup, just as the softmax upper bound copies the full sequence. The result therefore requires an explicit single-head scope and cannot support an arbitrary-h reading of c-size.

key_findings.claim: Communication size is a useful lower-bound resource but is not total model size, so 'concise' does not mean a polylogarithmic-parameter transformer.
key_findings.evidence: The definition hdp omits token and position embedding tables, the n-by-d unembedding, all MLP parameters, and even the number of MLP layers. The softmax upper bound explicitly delegates final evaluation to an MLP with n^{O(1)} parameters. A separate k-size lower bound includes MLP size but proves only n^epsilon for unspecified positive epsilon.

method.core_idea: Use function-table lookup as a minimal nonbinary computation, vary whether keys and values are colocated or positionally redundant, and derive matching shallow-transformer upper and lower bounds under explicit width-precision resources before comparing those boundaries with small-model trainability.
method.mechanism: Five layouts present an arbitrary map f:[n] to [n] plus a target key. Positive constructions encode symbols as points on a unit circle, use hard dot-product attention to select an exact key, and unembed the corresponding value. For the layout with permuted keys and separately positioned values, a two-party communication reduction yields an hdp lower bound for one-layer softmax transformers; a matching upper bound encodes the whole sequence in one attention output for a polynomial-size MLP. A second hard-attention layer supplies a constant-width alternative by binding adjacent keys and values. Experiments train one- and two-layer encoder-only softmax transformers with learned embeddings on randomly sampled permutation functions.
assumptions: The product of heads, embedding dimension, and numerical precision is the relevant resource for comparing shallow transformer expressivity, even though embeddings, unembedding, and MLP parameters are omitted.
The p-bit rational precision assumption permits rounding embeddings and head outputs without changing the transformer's discrete answer.
The input is a complete table over [n], keys are unique, and the target key occurs exactly once.
Hard-attention constructions are informative about learnable softmax transformers despite different embeddings, residuals, and optimization.
A family may use a separately designed transformer, positional encoding, vocabulary embedding, and unembedding for every n.
Permutation-valued functions are an adequate empirical proxy for the arbitrary functions quantified by the theorems.
Five seeds, best and mean final accuracy, and fixed training budget are sufficient to infer rough alignment between expressivity and learnability.

techniques.role: Isolates whether a layer must bind information across positions or can exploit positional redundancy.
Represents n discrete symbols in two dimensions with an inverse-polynomial dot-product gap and logarithmic precision.
Selects the unique matching key and copies its colocated value in a single head.
Converts one-layer evaluation into a message from the value holder to the key-permutation holder, giving an n log n bit lower bound.
Uses position one-hots and value-dependent softmax weights to copy the entire input into an O(n)-dimensional attention output.
Adds a precision-independent but weaker polynomial lower bound that accounts for the MLP.
Uses one layer to colocate adjacent key-value information and a second to retrieve the queried value.
Compares learned one- and two-layer softmax models across table sizes, embedding dimensions, layouts, and seeds.

evaluations.setting: Cases 1-4 at n=100; one attention layer, one head, learned token embeddings, optional learned positional embeddings, five seeds
evaluations.metric: Maximum and mean accuracy over 100 test batches after at most 10,000 training batches
evaluations.result: Models reach nearly 100% in at least one run when key-value information is colocated or positionally recoverable, while layouts requiring missing position information remain near 1% chance
evaluations.baseline: Ablation without positional embedding for cases 1 and 4; no hand-constructed model, alternate optimizer, sample-complexity curve, or arbitrary-function test

evaluations.setting: Difficult case 5 with n in {2,5,10,20}, one or two layers, and token dimension in {16,32,100,200}
evaluations.metric: Maximum and mean function-evaluation accuracy over five seeds
evaluations.result: Two layers dominate at many moderate-dimensional settings and can reach 100% at n=20, but both depths degrade sharply at large dimension and one layer can still reach nearly 100% for n at most 10
evaluations.baseline: One versus two attention layers under the same optimizer; no direct implementation of the constructive two-layer hard-attention solution

evaluations.setting: Per-seed distributions for cases 1-4 at n=100
evaluations.result: Several intermediate dimensions show bimodal runs near chance or near perfect accuracy
evaluations.baseline: Five seeds only; no mechanistic analysis of successful versus failed runs

limitations: Author-stated: expressivity is necessary but not sufficient for trainability, and the experiments show only rough alignment.
Author-stated: all tested one-layer difficult-case models are large enough to be compatible with the lower bound, so their failures do not empirically verify it.
Author-stated: the softmax upper bound uses much larger MLPs than the empirical models, which may explain failed training.
Author-stated: accuracy is strongly bimodal across seeds for several layouts and dimensions and the cause remains open.
Author-stated: the hard-attention constructions are not formally converted to standard softmax here; the paper only points to possible temperature-based simulation.
Reviewer-identified: empirical functions are permutations rather than arbitrary maps, so the experiment omits repeated output values and covers a strict subproblem.
Reviewer-identified: c-size omits potentially dominant embedding, unembedding, and MLP parameter counts, making the term concise narrower than ordinary model size.

Reviewer-identified: positive theory uses bespoke hard attention and analytic embeddings while experiments use learned softmax attention and residuals, preventing a controlled theory-to-practice comparison.
Reviewer-identified: Theorem 3.8's proof is single-head and cannot support an unrestricted multi-head impossibility reading.
Reviewer-identified: experiments report best-of-five results prominently despite large seed instability and do not quantify convergence time, loss, or confidence intervals.
Reviewer-identified: each n receives its own learned model and embedding tables; no length or vocabulary extrapolation is tested.
Reviewer-identified: the experimental MLP depth and width are not specified in the setup even though MLP capacity is central to the one-layer upper bound.
failure_modes: A one-layer head cannot associate a key token with a separately positioned value when their order is permuted and no positional redundancy identifies the pairing.
A model family can appear concise under hdp while storing linear or polynomial resources in embeddings, unembedding, or the MLP.
Hard-attention exact selectors can require temperature or margin scaling that ordinary softmax training never discovers.
Random initialization can fall into chance-level solutions even when a constant-dimensional exact construction exists.
Increasing embedding dimension can worsen optimization enough to erase the expected benefit of extra representational capacity.
Permutation-only data can reward mechanisms that rely on one-to-one values and fail on arbitrary many-to-one functions.
Best-seed accuracy can make a fragile learning regime look reliably solved.
A single-head impossibility can be misapplied to multi-head models that parallelize fixed-position retrieval.
reusable_insights: Factor synthetic transformer tasks by information layout, not only by abstract function; colocation and positional redundancy can change depth requirements.
State resource measures explicitly and report both communication size and total learned parameter or description length.
Pair asymptotic lower bounds with experiments whose tested models actually cross the predicted boundary.
Implement the constructive solution as an oracle and interpolate toward the trained architecture to identify which assumption causes optimization failure.
Test arbitrary functions, permutations, constant functions, and collision-heavy functions separately when evaluating lookup mechanisms.
Report full seed distributions and success probability for algorithmic tasks with bimodal training outcomes.
Audit impossibility theorems for head-count scope; parallel heads can turn a one-selection bottleneck into full-input access.
open_questions: What is the tight total-parameter lower bound when token embeddings, positional embeddings, unembedding, and MLPs all count?
Can gradient descent learn the explicit constant-width construction under softmax with a realistic fixed temperature and finite margin?
Does the two-layer advantage persist for arbitrary collision-heavy functions and unseen table sizes?
Which optimization mechanism creates the chance-versus-perfect bimodality, and can initialization or curriculum control it?
What are tight depth-head-width tradeoffs for the separated-and-permuted layout under multi-head hard attention?
Can a trainability theorem predict the sample and iteration complexity of binding adjacent keys and values?
How much of practical induction-head or factual-recall behavior is captured by complete-table function evaluation?

competitive_landscape.title: Are Transformers with One Layer Self-Attention Using Low-Rank Weight Matrices Universal Approximators?
competitive_landscape.difference: Kajitsuka and Sato prove one-layer finite-sample memorization and universal approximation with low-rank self-attention, but their generic construction can be enormous for a table-lookup family. This paper derives task-specific constant or linear communication-size constructions and matching layout-sensitive lower bounds.

competitive_landscape.title: Representational Strengths and Limitations of Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: Sanford, Hsu, and Telgarsky establish logarithmic advantages on sparse averaging and linear lower bounds on triple detection, foregrounding depth, width, and embedding dimension. The present work applies the same resource perspective to the more primitive operation of evaluating an in-context function table.

competitive_landscape.title: On Limitations of the Transformer Architecture
competitive_landscape.difference: Peng, Narayanan, and Papadimitriou use communication complexity to show one-layer limits for composing functions and provide probabilistic error bounds. The present paper strips composition down to one lookup, obtains a stronger representation-sensitive boundary, and corrects a missing sufficiently-large-n condition when reusing their lemma.

competitive_landscape.title: One-layer transformers fail to solve the induction heads task
competitive_landscape.difference: Sanford, Hsu, and Telgarsky prove an exponential one-versus-two-layer size separation for induction heads. This paper studies a complete-table lookup that generalizes the binding primitive and shows that the separation disappears when keys and values are colocated or positionally redundant.

competitive_landscape.title: Strassen Attention: Unlocking Compositional Abilities in Transformers Based on a New Lower Bound Method
competitive_landscape.difference: Kozachinskiy et al. use split VC dimension to prove lower bounds for one-layer softmax attention under exact real arithmetic and propose a higher-order attention alternative. The present paper imports that technique for a weaker n^epsilon total-size bound while its tight n log n result still relies on finite precision.

competitive_landscape.title: Theoretical limitations of multi-layer Transformer
competitive_landscape.difference: Chen, Peng, and Wu prove unconditional lower bounds for constant-depth decoder-only transformers on sequential composition and separate L from L+1 layers, encoders from decoders, and direct answers from chain of thought. This paper analyzes encoder-only single lookup with especially sharp input-layout dependence.

competitive_landscape.title: Understanding Factual Recall in Transformers via Associative Memories
competitive_landscape.difference: Nichani, Lee, and Bietti count all attention or MLP memory parameters for a synthetic factual-recall task and analyze gradient-flow learning in a simplified model. It addresses parameter-stored associations rather than arbitrary in-context tables, but offers a stronger bridge from expressivity to optimization than the present best-of-five sweeps.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims the first representation-sensitive characterization of the primitive function-evaluation task: concise one-layer transformers succeed in four layouts, require Theta(n log n) communication size in the separated-permuted layout, and regain concision with two layers, with experiments roughly matching these boundaries.
novelty_assessment.evidence: It supplies three constant-width lookup constructions, matching finite-precision one-layer bounds for the hard layout, a precision-independent polynomial lower bound, a constant-width two-layer construction, and trainability sweeps over all five layouts.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The sharp contribution is showing that cross-position binding, not lookup alone, creates the one-layer bottleneck, and matching the finite-precision communication lower bound with a task-specific upper bound. This is a useful refinement of prior induction-head and function-composition separations. The practical bridge is much weaker: experiments use permutation functions, different attention and embeddings, resource-rich models that do not straddle the bound, and unstable best-of-five outcomes. In addition, 'concise' excludes major parameter stores and the hard-attention impossibility needs explicit single-head scope. The theoretical layout taxonomy is strong; the learnability claim remains exploratory.

reviewer_notes: Read all seventeen extracted pages end to end, including every theorem, proof appendix, experimental table, violin plot, footnote, and reference. PDF page 7 was rendered and visually checked to resolve an extraction ambiguity in the softmax sequence-packing vector; the paper correctly indexes through v_(2n), so no off-by-one finding was recorded. The multi-head scope audit follows from the explicit one-head specialization on page 3 and the single-selected-output proof in Appendix E. Current competitors were checked on primary arXiv and OpenReview records on 2026-08-23 across communication complexity, one-layer universality, induction heads, precision-independent bounds, multi-layer limits, and associative recall.
